newsitem.title: FINLAND: WAGE FLEXIBILITY TOUGH NUT IF FINLAND JOINS EMU.
newsitem.headline: WAGE FLEXIBILITY TOUGH NUT IF FINLAND JOINS EMU.

text.p: By joining EMU, Finland will lose the option of restoring industry's competitiveness through devaluation and economists say this will demand flexible wages and may change the collective bargaining system.

But Finland's by European measures highly organised workers say, through their vocal and sometimes militant unions, they will accept neither downward wage flexibility nor a scrapping of centralised pay bargaining.
"It could have a disastrous effect if wages were determined according to supply and demand," said Jarmo Lahteenmaki, leader of the influential Paper Workers' Union.
The union was critical to EMU but wanted more information before deciding its stance, he said.
Employers support Finland's stated objective to join the third stage of Economic and Monetary Union due to begin in January 1999.
"Wages and other labour costs would have to adjust to cyclical changes once Finland is in EMU," said economist Simo Pinomaa at the Confederation of Finnish Industry and Employers.
He and other economists say Finland's incomes settlement system with centralised collective bargaining must be overhauled once Finland becomes part of the single Euro currency.
The first step would be a move to sectoral agreements. The forest industry, for example, would negotiate its own pay deals.
Currently, Finnish employer federations and unions engage in branch-by-branch pay talks if centralised bargaining talks fail.
"It seems very likely that incomes agreements will be settled at branch level in the future," Martti Hetemaki, head of the finance ministry's economics department, told a seminar recently.

"If EMU means an end to centralised incomes bargaining then we will not be part of it," said Pertti Parmanne, chief economist at the Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK), an umbrella for mostly blue-collar branch unions representing some 1.1 million workers.
"I am sure there are some who will use EMU as an excuse to move away from centralised pay deals," Parmanne said.
But Hannu Kaseva, analyst at the Research Institute of the Finnish Economy (ETLA), went even further.
He expected salaries and oter terms of employment to be agreed at an even more decentralised level, company by company, once Finland entered the third stage of EMU.
"EMU will force wage deals to be settled at the company level rather than through centralised or branch agreements," Kaseva said.

"The labour markets must learn to adapt to cyclical changes more swiftly in the future, the other option is that entire sectors will do downtime and that could be catastrophic in a small economy like Finland," he added.

So far, the five-party left-right-green government, which has staked its reputation on close cooperation with trade unions and other social partners, has kept mostly silent on the issue of wage flexibility in an EMU environment.
Social democratic Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen has spoken in favour of setting up special funds which EMU member countries could draw on in cyclical downturns.
"It is an extremely sensitive issue for the government as it tries to maintain a national consenus regarding EMU," said one economist, requesting anonymity.
